# 6.3 Active vs. Passive Investing: Key file (for the AI tutor only)

Do not reveal anything here before the learner has answered.

## Lesson facts relevant to the questions

- The learner has studied the normal distribution (Lesson 0.4, "Distributions and Statistical Inference" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/0-4-distributions-inference/), beta, $R^2$ and the single-index model (Lesson 4.4, "The Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM)" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/4-4-capm/, Lesson 4.5, "The Single-Index Model and Estimating Beta" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/4-5-single-index-model/), factor models (Lesson 4.6, "Multifactor Models" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/4-6-multifactor-models/), market efficiency (Lesson 4.7, "The Efficient Market Hypothesis" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/4-7-market-efficiency/), performance evaluation, luck versus skill and survivorship bias (Lesson 4.9, "Performance Evaluation" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/4-9-performance-evaluation/), credit spreads (Lesson 3.6, "Credit Risk" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/3-6-credit-risk/) and fund types and costs (Lesson 6.1, "Fund Types and Structures" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/6-1-fund-types/, Lesson 6.2, "Fund Costs" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/6-2-fund-costs/). Percentages in percentage points.
- The lesson: Sharpe's (1991) arithmetic: passive investors earn the market return before costs; all investors together hold the market portfolio, so active investors as a group also earn only the market return before costs, $\bar{R}_A = R_M - c_A$ (money-weighted); active investing is zero-sum among active investors; the result does not depend on market efficiency. The lesson does not discuss a changing passive share (left to Exercises Question 1).
- The lesson: SPIVA U.S. Scorecard (year-end 2024), shares lagging: large-cap (S&P 500) over 1/5/10/15/20 years 65.2%, 76.3%, 84.3%, 89.5%, 92.0%; mid-cap 62.0%, 80.0%, 77.3%, 87.5%, 90.9%; small-cap 29.7%, 60.4%, 82.2%, 90.7%, 90.8%. Liquidated or merged funds are included as not beating; benchmarks match style. About 36% of US stock funds from 20 years earlier survived to end-2024. In 2025 about 79% of active large-cap funds lagged the S&P 500 (SPIVA year-end 2025).
- The lesson: a fund with no skill has yearly excess returns averaging $-f$ with standard deviation $\sigma$ (tracking error), independent and normal; the probability of beating cumulatively over $T$ years is $P = N\left(-\frac{f\sqrt{T}}{\sigma}\right)$. Figure 3-1: horizontal axis 1–30 years; sliders cost 0–2% (steps of 0.25, default 1) and tracking error 2–10% (steps of 1, default 5); by default about 42.1%, 26.4%, 18.6% at 1, 10, 20 years; with tracking error 10%, about 46.0%, 37.6%, 32.7%.
- The lesson: SPIVA Persistence Scorecard (year-end 2025): of 505 US stock funds in the top quarter in December 2021, none stayed in the top quarter every year through December 2025; random would give about $\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)^4 \approx 0.4\%$ (about 2 funds); of 1,010 top-half funds, 7.92% stayed in the top half 4 years running, against 6.25% if random. The lesson draws no conclusion (left to Check C4).
- The lesson: factsheets list expense ratio, size, inception, benchmark, top ten holdings, sector and region breakdown, style box, returns against the benchmark and risk statistics (standard deviation, beta, $R^2$, tracking error, Sharpe ratio); the prospectus summary gives the objective, fee table, principal strategies and risks, past returns against an index and the managers; the SAI has brokerage commissions and managers' own investment; annual and semiannual reports give full holdings, financial statements and turnover. Active share $AS = \frac{1}{2}\sum_i |w_i - w_i^B|$ (Cremers and Petajisto, 2009): 0 means identical to the benchmark, 100% no overlap.

## Check question C1

If there are enough active managers and they are clever enough, active investors as a group can beat the market after costs.

Correct answer: False

Hint (give it after a wrong answer, without the verdict): What do active and passive investors hold together? What do passive investors earn before costs? What, then, do active investors as a group earn before costs?

**Reference answer**

False. All investors together hold the market portfolio and passive investors earn the market return, so active investors as a group can also earn only the market return before costs; after their higher costs, the group must lag. Cleverness only decides who wins and who loses among active investors; it cannot change the group's average.

## Check question C2

In 2024 only about 30% of US active small-cap funds lagged the S&P SmallCap 600, but over 20 years about 91% lagged. The most reasonable reading of the 2024 result is:

- (A) One year's result is very noisy and may come from differences in style or size between funds and the index that happened to pay off that year; it does not show lasting skill among small-cap managers ← Correct answer
- (B) The small-cap market is inefficient, so investors should choose actively managed small-cap funds
  Why it is wrong (tell the learner when they choose this option): If excess returns were easy in small caps, why do more than 80% lag over 10, 15 and 20 years?
- (C) SPIVA changed its method in 2024
  Why it is wrong (tell the learner when they choose this option): The 1-year and 20-year figures come from the same report and the same method. The likely explanation lies in the funds and the index themselves.

**Reference answer**

(A). One year's excess return is driven mainly by noise and style differences: for example many "small-cap" funds hold larger companies than those in the S&P SmallCap 600, and when those stocks do well in a year, most funds beat the index. Long-run results say more about costs and skill: about 91% lag over 20 years. Picking one good year to prove that a kind of active management works is choosing the favorable one out of many possible comparisons (multiple testing).

## Check question C3

In Figure 3-1, keep the cost at 1% and raise the tracking error from 5% to 10%. The probability that a fund with no skill beats the index over 20 years:

- (A) Rises, because larger random deviations let more funds with no skill win by chance ← Correct answer
- (B) Falls, because riskier funds find it harder to win
  Why it is wrong (tell the learner when they choose this option): In the formula $\sigma$ is in the denominator. When $\sigma$ grows, does $-\frac{f\sqrt{T}}{\sigma}$ move closer to 0 or further from it?
- (C) Stays the same, because a fund with no skill always lags by its cost on average
  Why it is wrong (tell the learner when they choose this option): The average lag is indeed unchanged, but the probability also depends on how spread out the outcomes are. Look at the readout in the figure.

**Reference answer**

(A). It rises from about 18.6% to 32.7%. The average lag is still 1% a year, but a larger tracking error spreads outcomes more, so more of them fall on the winning side. Funds that stray further from their benchmark therefore produce more lucky winners in their long-run records, making it harder to judge skill from a winning record alone (Lesson 4.9, "Performance Evaluation" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/4-9-performance-evaluation/).

## Check question C4

For the SPIVA persistence result (none of 505 top-quarter funds stayed in the top quarter for 4 years in a row, against about 2 if random), the most reasonable conclusion is:

- (A) Past high rankings barely predict future high rankings; the result is consistent with luck dominating ← Correct answer
- (B) Top-ranked managers lose their skill after succeeding
  Why it is wrong (tell the learner when they choose this option): If rankings are mostly luck, this result appears without anyone "losing skill". What evidence could tell the two explanations apart?
- (C) Investors should switch each year to the previous year's top-ranked fund
  Why it is wrong (tell the learner when they choose this option): If last year's ranking does not predict next year's, what does chasing the top fund each year achieve? What extra costs does it bring?

**Reference answer**

(A). With purely random rankings about 2 funds would be expected to stay on top; the actual number is 0, and the top-half result (7.92%) is only slightly above the random 6.25%. Past rankings have almost no power to predict future ones. The result is even slightly below random, perhaps because of style rotation: funds at the top in one year often bet on a style that then falls behind when styles change. This does not prove no manager has skill, but it shows that picking funds by past rankings is of little use.

## Check question C5

An active large-cap fund has an expense ratio of 0.90%, an $R^2$ of 0.99 relative to the S&P 500 and an active share of 20%. The most reasonable judgment about this fund is:

- (A) Its holdings and returns are very close to the index, so investors pay active fees for a portfolio that is mostly the index ← Correct answer
- (B) The high $R^2$ shows the manager picks stocks accurately
  Why it is wrong (tell the learner when they choose this option): $R^2$ measures the share of the fund's return explained by the index. What does 0.99 say about how different the fund's return is from the index?
- (C) An active share of 20% means the fund earns about 20% more than the index each year
  Why it is wrong (tell the learner when they choose this option): Active share is computed from holdings weights; it measures how different the holdings are from the benchmark, not the return.

**Reference answer**

(A). An active share of 20% means about 80% of the holdings overlap the index, and an $R^2$ of 0.99 means the return moves almost entirely with the index. Such funds are often called closet indexers: only about 20% of the portfolio reflects active choices, yet 0.90% is charged on all assets. Charged against the truly active part, the fee is about $\frac{0.90\% - 0.03\%}{20\%} \approx 4.4\%$ a year, which that part's stock picking would find very hard to make up.

## Exercises Question 1 (id: Q1)

Suppose 40% of the stock market's assets are held by index funds with a total cost of 0.05% a year, and 60% by active investors with an average total cost (fees and trading costs) of 0.80% a year.
(a) Weighted by money, do active investors earn more or less than the market after costs, and by how much?
(b) A fund manager says: "As passive investing grows, fewer people are looking for mispricing, so active investors as a group have a growing chance to beat the market." Evaluate this statement. Under what circumstances might "passive investors" earn something other than the market return even before costs?

**Reference answer**

(a) Before costs active investors as a group earn the market return, so after costs they lag the market by 0.8 percentage points on average (−0.8%), and index investors by 0.75 percentage points. This holds whether passive investing is 40% or 90%.
(b) The statement is wrong, at least for the group. As long as passive investors hold the market portfolio, active investors as a group earn the market return before costs, however large the passive share. More passive investing may leave more mispricing and make it easier for an individual capable manager to profit, but those profits come from other active investors' losses; active investing is still zero-sum among active investors, and the group still lags by its costs. In reality "passive investors" are not fully passive (Pedersen, 2018): when an index changes its members, index funds must trade according to published rules, and active investors trading ahead can profit; new issues, secondary offerings and buybacks keep changing the market portfolio, so index funds must trade. In such cases passive investors may earn slightly less than the true market return before costs and active investors as a group slightly more; but the amount is small, far smaller than the average cost of active management.

**Grading points**

- (a) OK: active investors lag the market by 0.8 percentage points after costs on average, independent of the passive share.
- (b) OK: says that as long as passive investors hold the market portfolio, active investors as a group still earn the market return before costs, and individual managers' gains come from other active investors; gives at least one way passive investors are not fully passive (index changes, new issues, etc.). Agreeing that the group's chances grow needs revision.

Numeric answers: gap = -0.8

**Common errors**

- Thinking that the more passive investing there is, the less efficient markets become, so active investors as a group must beat the market; ignoring that by definition active investors as a group still earn the market return before costs.

## Exercises Question 2 (id: Q2)

An intermediate core bond fund is benchmarked to the Bloomberg US Aggregate Bond Index. In 2024 it beat its benchmark by 0.6 percentage points. On average it held 20 percentage points more corporate bonds than the benchmark (and correspondingly fewer Treasuries), with the same interest rate risk (duration) as the benchmark; that year corporate bonds earned 2.5 percentage points more than Treasuries after removing the effect of rates.
(a) Roughly how much of the excess return came from the extra corporate bonds?
(b) The fund's marketing says: "Our managers beat the benchmark through excellent judgment." Evaluate this statement. In what kind of year would this approach lag the benchmark?

**Reference answer**

(a) About $20\% \times 2.5\% = 0.5$ percentage points, most of the 0.6 percentage points of excess return.
(b) The statement is misleading. Most of the excess return comes from bearing more credit risk all the time (Lesson 3.6, "Credit Risk" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/3-6-credit-risk/): the benchmark holds fewer corporate bonds, the fund systematically overweights them, and the extra credit spread is pay for bearing default and liquidity risk, not bond-picking skill. Investors could get the same exposure cheaply with a corporate bond index fund. In years when credit spreads widen (such as 2008 and March 2020), corporate bonds lag Treasuries and such a fund lags its benchmark clearly, often just when stocks are falling too. Such funds should be judged against a benchmark or regression that includes a credit factor (Lesson 4.6, "Multifactor Models" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/4-6-multifactor-models/), to see whether any excess return remains after the credit exposure. This is partly why in the SPIVA reports most investment-grade bond funds beat their benchmarks over one year.

**Grading points**

- (a) OK: about 0.5 percentage points.
- (b) OK: says the excess comes mainly from systematically bearing more credit risk, which is pay for risk, not skill; explains it lags when credit spreads widen; mentioning evaluation after controlling for credit exposure is a plus. Agreeing it was judgment needs revision.

Numeric answers: credit = 0.5

**Common errors**

- Taking excess return over a benchmark as manager skill; ignoring that the fund may bear risks the benchmark does not (such as more credit risk), so the excess is pay for those risks.

## Exercises Question 3 (id: Q3)

Twenty years ago a fund company had 100 stock funds; 36 still exist and the rest were liquidated or merged. Of the 36 survivors, 25% beat their benchmarks over the 20 years.
(a) If none of the liquidated or merged funds beat its benchmark, what percentage of the original 100 funds beat their benchmarks?
(b) The company's advertisement says: "25% of our long-term funds beat their benchmarks, far better than the industry average." Evaluate this statement. Why are liquidated funds mostly poor performers?

**Reference answer**

(a) $36 \times 25\% = 9$ funds, or 9%.
(b) The statement is misleading. 25% is the share among survivors only, which suffers from survivorship bias (Lesson 4.9, "Performance Evaluation" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/4-9-performance-evaluation/): the 64 liquidated or merged funds have vanished from the count. Counting all the funds of 20 years ago, only 9% beat their benchmarks, close to SPIVA's roughly 8% for large-cap funds over 20 years (92% lagging), so no better than the industry. Fund companies tend to close or merge poor performers, because such funds lose money to outflows, shrink until revenue falls below cost, and drag down the company's overall record; merged into a good fund, the bad record disappears. SPIVA counts liquidated funds as not beating precisely to avoid this bias.

**Grading points**

- (a) OK: 9%.
- (b) OK: names survivorship bias, notes only 9% of all funds beat, similar to the industry; explains that poor funds are closed or merged because of outflows, shrinking size and damage to the record. Agreeing with the ad needs revision.

Numeric answers: share = 9

**Common errors**

- Judging the success rate of active management from surviving funds only; ignoring liquidated and merged funds (survivorship bias).

## Exercises Question 4 (id: Q4)

A "growth fund" factsheet shows: benchmark the S&P 500; over the past 10 years the fund returned 13% a year and the S&P 500 12%; the fund's beta is 1.2, its $R^2$ relative to the S&P 500 is 0.85, and its standard deviation 20% (15% for the S&P 500); expense ratio 0.75%. The risk-free rate averaged 2% over the period.
(a) By CAPM (Lesson 4.4, "The Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM)" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/4-4-capm/), what is the fund's Jensen alpha, roughly?
(b) The fund advertises that it "beats its benchmark by 1 percentage point a year". Evaluate this statement, and say what else should be looked at and against which benchmark.

**Reference answer**

(a) CAPM requires $2\% + 1.2 \times (12\% - 2\%) = 14\%$, so alpha is about $13\% - 14\% = -1\%$.
(b) The statement is misleading. With a beta of 1.2 the fund bore 20% more market risk than the S&P 500; in a decade of rising markets the higher beta alone should have earned 2 percentage points more, but the fund earned only 1 more, so it lagged after adjusting for risk. An $R^2$ of 0.85 means a good part of the return is not explained by the S&P 500: the fund's style (growth) differs from the S&P 500, and a better benchmark is a growth index (such as the S&P 500 Growth) or a regression with size, value and momentum factors (Lesson 4.6, "Multifactor Models" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/4-6-multifactor-models/). One should also look at: the t-statistic of alpha, since 10 years of data usually cannot separate luck from skill (Lesson 4.9, "Performance Evaluation" https://ianding1.github.io/ai-tutored-finance/en/lessons/4-9-performance-evaluation/); whether growth stocks as a whole happened to do very well in these 10 years; whether the manager ran the fund the whole time; and whether fees are already deducted (they are, since returns are computed from NAV).

**Grading points**

- (a) OK: required return 14%, alpha about −1%.
- (b) OK: says the higher beta explains the excess and it lags after adjusting for risk; says $R^2$ and style show the benchmark is unsuitable and a growth index or factor regression should be used; mentions at least one of statistical significance or manager tenure. Agreeing it beats by 1 percentage point needs revision.

Numeric answers: alpha = -1

**Common errors**

- Judging a fund to have won because its return beat the benchmark; ignoring that its beta and style differ from the benchmark, so the comparison should be risk-adjusted against a suitable benchmark.
